storm.summary_layperson: Strong storm cells are visible on radar to the north, but they're tracking away from the cove rather than toward it, so no storm arrival is expected here this evening.
storm.local_effect_blurb: These storms are approaching from over land to the north rather than crossing the cool Sound, so the cove's usual storm-weakening marine layer isn't a factor either way.
storm.detail_html:
An Air Quality Alert is in effect regionally, and the NWS Area Forecast Discussion (issued 3:43 PM) flags pop-up shower and thunderstorm potential through early evening, driven by a deep cold pool aloft and a weak surface high that isn't providing much sinking-air suppression. The AFD also notes 30–40 kt of bulk shear in the lowest 6 km, enough for a marginal severe risk. Locally, instability is moderate (CAPE 1030 J/kg) and shear sits at 30.1 kt from the NNW — the gray zone (20–35 kt) where the outcome depends on how organized the storms actually are.

Radar (KOKX) shows cells reaching 55 dBZ, all positioned north to northwest of the cove between 32 and 49 miles out. Tracking the reflectivity centroid across two scans measures the system moving WNW at 38 kt — away from Greenwich, not toward it. Every tracked cell shows a negative closing speed ("moving away"), so the arrival-prediction engine has no closing cell and no ETA to report for the cove tonight.

The Sound's protective marine layer is present (a moderate 9°F air-water temperature difference, water at 73°F vs air at 82°F) but isn't the reason for the quiet outlook here — it simply isn't in play, because these storms are approaching from due north over land rather than crossing the Sound. That's why tonight's local effect reads as neutral rather than mitigating: the mechanism this skill exists to catch isn't relevant to this particular storm track.

Net for the cove vs. surrounding areas: as of this snapshot, the storm activity currently sitting to the north may clip towns closer to it, while the immediate coastline at Greenwich stays dry and calm. That said, the AFD's "pop-up" language through early evening means new cells could still form closer to home later in the window — CAPE (1030 J/kg, trending toward roughly 1500 J/kg in later HRRR hours) stays well under the 3000 J/kg punch-through threshold, so any new development would likely still be capped rather than explosive. Watch for a new cell appearing to the west or northwest and beginning to close — that would flip this call.

wind.tactics_blurb: Sea-breeze day out of the SSW, building to a peak around 6-7 PM before fading fast after sunset (8:11 PM). Pressure is fairly even across the cove tonight; play the oscillations rather than banging a corner, and don't expect much left on the water after 9.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
Today is a pure thermal sea breeze day, not a gradient-wind day. The two ingredients line up: the air–water temperature difference is a strong 9.2°F (7.0°F from the buoy pairing), and the background synoptic wind is light and roughly westerly (NWS grid forecast: "West wind around 3 mph"; the region-wide authoritative station mean is 6.6 kt) — calm/offshore enough that it isn't reinforcing or fighting the thermal. In the western Long Island Sound zone specifically (Riverside YC, the 44040 buoy, and the Old Greenwich/Port Chester APRS cluster), 70% of stations are already running southerly with a median direction of SSW 193° and 0.7 direction agreement — a locally well-established sea breeze even though the wider regional fractions (which mix in New Haven and Long Island stations) look more muted.

HRRR's raw hour-by-hour surface direction is noisy right now (it swings from S to ENE to SSE hour to hour) because modeled wind speeds are all under 5 kt in this window — direction is poorly constrained at that speed. Riverside YC and the western-LIS ensemble are the more trustworthy read: currently S/SSW around 188-193° at 6-9 kt. HRRR's f01 call of S 182° is 11° backed from the observed 193°, and since the sea breeze is mature (deltaT above 8°F, mid-afternoon and later), the maturation correction adds roughly 15° of veer for the forecast hours, landing on a corrected SSW ~197° — that's the direction used for the 5-10 PM window above rather than HRRR's raw, noisier numbers.

Cove geography for SSW flow is about as clean as it gets here: fairly uniform pressure across the whole course, with maybe a touch more breeze right at the mouth and on the east side (less shelter from Tod's Point in this direction) than tucked against the west shore. Nothing pronounced enough to bank on one side — play the boat, not the map.

Shift character: this is now a mature sea breeze (well past the ramping phase that ended mid-afternoon), so expect the classic 5–15 minute oscillations of roughly 10–20° each side of the SSW mean — tack on the headers rather than committing to a corner. That holds through the peak around 6-7 PM. Sunset is 8:11 PM; per the standard sea-breeze collapse rule, expect the thermal to fade within 30-60 minutes of sunset. The table above builds that in: softening starts around 8 PM, and by 9-10 PM speeds drop under 5 kt with direction going light and unreliable as the driving mechanism shuts off.

For the fleet: 6-8 kt through the first half of the window is the sweet spot for one-design dinghies — good, honest racing. By 9 PM it's drifter territory, and by 10 PM there may not be enough pressure to finish a race cleanly. Plan the last start accordingly.
